- However, your inductive step does not justify the crucial reduction. To apply the induction hypothesis, you must show:

  2) The next person to be counted is 1. This needs an argument: the last eliminated in the first pass is 2^{n+1} (even), which is adjacent to 1, so counting resumes at 1.

- Introduce the bijection 2j−1 ↦ j and justify that it turns the problem on 2^{n+1} into the same problem on 2^n starting at 1.

- You correctly show that there is no largest natural number: if B were maximal, then B+1 ∈ N and B+1 > B, a contradiction. This part is fine (use “>” rather than “≥” for precision).

Main issue:
- “No largest element” does not by itself imply “not bounded above.” A set can be bounded above without attaining its supremum (e.g. {x ∈ R : x < 0} has no maximum but is bounded above by 0). So the final step “hence the natural numbers are unbounded” is not justified from your argument as written.

- Derive a contradiction from the assumption that N is bounded above. Two standard routes:
  1) Supremum approach: Assume N is bounded above and let s = sup N. Using the supremum property with ε = 1, pick n ∈ N with s − 1 < n ≤ s. Then n + 1 ∈ N and n + 1 > s, contradicting that s is an upper bound.

Summary: Your overall idea—argue by contradiction that assuming nx ≤ y forces a bound on N—is along the right lines, but (i) the detour through absolute values is unnecessary and causes errors, and (ii) the key step relies on an unproved fact equivalent to what you are trying to prove. test.llm_feedback:
Helpful feedback:

- Good start: You moved to polar coordinates and decomposed the velocity into radial and tangential components using the fixed geometric angle π/N. This recognizes the underlying symmetry of the pursuit.

- Missing justification: You should explicitly argue that the configuration remains a shrinking regular N-gon, so the angular separation α = 2π/N is constant, and that each dog’s velocity makes angle α/2 = π/N with the tangent. This self-similarity is key.

- Dimensional/kinematic error in θ̇: From the tangential (orthoradial) component, v cos(π/N) is the tangential speed, which equals r θ̇, not θ̇ itself. Thus
  θ̇ = v cos(π/N) / r,
  not θ̇ = v cos(π/N). A quick units check reveals your expression has the wrong dimensions.

- Radial component: Your use of the radial component corresponds to ṙ = −v sin(π/N), which is correct (and constant in time).

- Eliminating t: Because θ̇ has the 1/r factor, the correct relation is
  dr/dθ = (ṙ)/(θ̇) = −r tan(π/N),
  not a constant. Missing this r factor led you to a linear r(θ) instead of the correct logarithmic dependence.

- Consequence for the path: Integrating dr/dθ = −r tan(π/N) yields an exponential in θ (a logarithmic spiral), not the linear function you obtained. Your initial-condition handling (introducing θ0 with r(θ0) = R) is fine and should be retained, but it will fix a multiplicative constant rather than an additive one.

- Presentation tip: When you say “orthoradial component,” make the relation to tangential speed explicit: v_tan = r θ̇. Also briefly justify why the angle to the tangent is π/N by symmetry.

If you make these corrections—justify the constant geometry, use r θ̇ for the tangential speed, and carry the r through when eliminating t—you will arrive at the correct logarithmic spiral with the right dependence on θ and the correct initial constant.
